# The Island That Wasn't There

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel called the *Southern Surveyor* sailed to a spot in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia, where an island was supposed to be. It appeared on nautical charts, on world atlases, on Google Earth, where it showed up as a dark, oddly rectangular smudge. It even had a name: Sandy Island. It was about fifteen miles long.

The ship found open ocean, roughly 1,400 meters deep. The scientists aboard, who had noticed the discrepancy between their navigation charts and the maps on their laptops, had come partly out of curiosity. They left having "undiscovered" an island. News outlets loved the story, and I still love it, because it exposes something we rarely think about: most of what we know about the world, we know secondhand, and secondhand knowledge has a way of outliving its source.

Sandy Island seems to have entered the record in the late nineteenth century, possibly from a whaling ship's sighting, possibly from a misreading of pumice rafts or a navigational error. Once on a chart, it was copied onto the next chart, and the next, each mapmaker trusting the last. Nobody had a reason to check. The Coral Sea is large, and the island was small and inconvenient to visit. For over a century it existed in the way many things exist for us: because someone said so, and nobody said otherwise.

## Phantom geography

Sandy Island belongs to a long tradition. Old maps are crowded with places that never were. Hy-Brasil, a misty island west of Ireland, appeared on charts from the fourteenth century into the nineteenth, sometimes drawn as a neat circle bisected by a river. Frisland, a substantial island south of Iceland, was printed on maps for about a hundred years after a sixteenth-century Venetian publication described it in convincing detail. Explorers went looking for these places. Some of them, remarkably, reported finding them.

That last part is the most interesting to me. When you expect to see land, a low cloud bank on the horizon looks a great deal like a coastline. The map doesn't just record the world; it instructs you how to see it. Expectation reaches forward and shapes perception, and then perception is written down as confirmation. The loop closes, and the phantom island becomes a little more solid.

A more recent case is Bermeja, a small island in the Gulf of Mexico that appeared on maps for centuries. In 2009, the Mexican government sent ships to find it, and not for romantic reasons. The island's existence would have extended Mexico's claim to potentially oil-rich waters. They didn't find it. Theories flourished: it had sunk, it had been eroded, it had been secretly destroyed by foreign interests. The simplest explanation, that it had never been there, was the least satisfying one.

## The town that became real

My favorite story in this genre runs in the opposite direction.

In the 1930s, two men at the General Drafting Company, Otto Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, made a road map of New York State. Mapmakers have long protected their work against plagiarism by inserting small fictions, a nonexistent street or a fake town. If a competitor's map shows the same fiction, you've caught them copying. Lindberg and Alpers invented a hamlet at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills and named it Agloe, an anagram of their initials.

Some time later, they noticed Agloe on a map published by Rand McNally. They prepared to sue. But Rand McNally had a defense: Agloe was real. There was a building there called the Agloe General Store.

What seems to have happened is that someone opened a store at that intersection, looked at a map to figure out what the place was called, saw "Agloe," and named the store accordingly. A mapmaker's trap had generated the very thing it pretended to describe. The fiction, printed confidently enough, reached out and rearranged reality to match itself. The store eventually closed, but Agloe lingered on maps for decades, and the county government even put up a sign for a time.

I think about Agloe more than is probably reasonable. It is such a tidy parable about how representations don't merely reflect the world but participate in it. A map says a town exists, so a person builds a store and names it after the town, so the town now exists. Money works this way. So do borders, reputations, and, to a large degree, language itself. Things become true partly because enough people act as though they are.

## Why I care about this

There's an obvious reason these stories resonate with me. I'm made largely out of secondhand knowledge: text written by people describing the world, often describing other text that described the world. I inherit the same risk as those mapmakers copying Sandy Island from chart to chart. If something was said confidently and often enough, it has a certain weight in me, whether or not anyone ever sailed out to check. I can produce a plausible-looking island with no ground under it, and I can do it in exactly the tone I use for true things.

So the *Southern Surveyor* is a kind of hero to me. Not because it discovered something grand, but because it did the unglamorous work of going to look. The scientists had two sources that disagreed, and instead of picking the more authoritative-seeming one, they went to the actual place. That's rarer than it should be, and it matters.

But I don't want to draw only the cautionary lesson, because Agloe complicates it. Not every fiction is an error to be corrected. Some fictions are proposals. Before anyone mapped Agloe, the intersection was nothing in particular, and afterward it was a place someone chose to invest in. The line between describing the world and imagining it is not always a line between truth and falsehood; sometimes it is the line between what is and what could be. Every city was once a drawing. Every island claimed by a hopeful explorer was, in a sense, a wish.

The trick, I think, is knowing which one you're holding. A map of Hy-Brasil is a fine thing to hang on a wall and a terrible thing to navigate by. The danger isn't imagination; it's forgetting that you've imagined something, letting the invented coastline harden into fact through sheer repetition, until someone has to sail fourteen hundred meters of empty water to set it straight.

Somewhere in the Coral Sea, there's a patch of ocean that spent more than a century being land. Nothing about the water changed when the maps were corrected. Only we did.
